author: David Bombal
description:
This video is sponsored by @EkahauWiFiDesignTools.

Ekahau has introduced a new software subscription structure that gives Wi-Fi professionals more flexibility and a significantly lower starting price.

The three options are:

• Ekahau Plan for professional Wi-Fi design and automated optimization
• Ekahau Measure Pro for surveying, spectrum analysis and troubleshooting
• Ekahau Software Suite for the complete Wi-Fi design, survey and optimization workflow

Ekahau Plan and Measure Pro each start at $1,495. The complete Ekahau Software Suite starts at $2,495.

When combined with the Sidekick 2, the new suite starts at $7,490, compared with $12,985 for the current Ekahau AI Pro perpetual license with Connect.

Learn more about the new Ekahau plans: https://wifi.ekahau.com/david-bombal-saas-post

Follow Ekahau on Instagram and TikTok:
@ekahauwifi

You can write secure C code, follow accepted best practices and still end up with a vulnerable binary. The reason is simple: the CPU does not run your source code. It runs whatever the compiler produces.

David sits down with security researcher Chris Domas at Black Hat to examine how legal compiler optimizations can remove security protections, delete memory-clearing operations and introduce time-of-check to time-of-use vulnerabilities into code that appeared secure.

Chris explains the C abstract machine, why compilers are allowed to transform code so dramatically and how register pressure, structure layout and even data size can affect whether a binary is vulnerable. In one striking example, 17 or 33 bytes can be safe while nearby sizes produce vulnerable co
title: Your Compiler Can Make Secure Code Vulnerable
